# 2 Samuel Chapter 12 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 180v–181v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_012_page_001.jpg, 2SA_012_page_002.jpg, 2SA_012_page_003.jpg

---

**1** The LORD sent Nathan to David. He came to him and said:

"There were two men in a certain town — one rich, one poor. **2** The rich man owned vast flocks and herds. **3** But the poor man had nothing at all except one small ewe lamb he had bought and raised. She grew up with him and his children. She ate from his plate, drank from his cup, and slept in his arms. She was like a daughter to him.

**4** One day a traveler arrived at the rich man's home. But the rich man couldn't bring himself to take an animal from his own flocks or herds to feed his guest. Instead, he took the poor man's lamb and served it to his visitor."

**5** David exploded with anger at the man. "As surely as the LORD lives," he said to Nathan, "the man who did this deserves to die! **6** He must pay for that lamb four times over — because he did this thing and had no pity."

**7** Then Nathan said to David, "You are the man!

"This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'I anointed you king over Israel. I rescued you from Saul's power. **8** I gave you your master's household and put your master's wives in your arms. I gave you all of Israel and Judah. And if all that had not been enough, I would have given you even more.

**9** Why did you treat the LORD's word with contempt and do what is evil in his sight? You struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword. You took his wife as your own. You had him murdered by the Ammonites.

**10** Because of this, the sword will never leave your household — because you treated me with contempt and took the wife of Uriah the Hittite for yourself.'

**11** "This is what the LORD says: 'I am going to bring disaster on you from within your own family. Before your very eyes I will take your wives and hand them over to someone close to you, and he will sleep with your wives in broad daylight. **12** What you did in secret, I will do in the open — before all Israel, under the open sky.'"

**13** David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the LORD."

Nathan replied, "The LORD has taken away your sin. You will not die. **14** But because you have treated the LORD with utter contempt by doing this, the son born to you will die."

**15** Then Nathan went home. And the LORD struck the child that Uriah's wife had borne to David, and the boy became very ill.

**16** David begged God for the child's life. He fasted and went inside and spent the night lying on the bare ground. **17** The elders of his household came and stood over him, trying to get him up from the ground. But he refused, and he would not eat anything with them.

**18** On the seventh day, the child died. David's servants were afraid to tell him the child was dead. They said to each other, "While the child was still alive, we tried to talk to him and he wouldn't listen. How can we possibly tell him the child is dead? He might do something desperate."

**19** David noticed his servants whispering among themselves and realized the child was dead. "Is the child dead?" he asked. "Yes," they answered. "He is dead."

**20** David got up from the ground. He bathed, put on lotions, and changed his clothes. He went to the house of the LORD and worshiped. Then he went home and asked for food. When they placed it before him, he ate.

**21** His servants said to him, "What are you doing? While the child was alive, you fasted and wept. But the moment the child died, you got up and ate!"

**22** David answered, "While the child was alive, I fasted and wept because I thought, 'Who knows? Maybe the LORD will be gracious to me and let the child live.' **23** But now he's dead. Why should I go on fasting? Can I bring him back? I will go to him one day, but he will never come back to me."

**24** David comforted his wife Bathsheba. He went to her and made love to her, and she gave birth to a son. David named him Solomon. And the LORD loved the boy. **25** He sent word through Nathan the prophet, who named him Jedidiah — "Beloved of the LORD" — because the LORD loved him.

**26** Meanwhile, Joab was still fighting against Rabbah of the Ammonites and had captured the royal fortress. **27** He sent messengers to David with this report: "I have attacked Rabbah and have taken control of the water supply. **28** Now assemble the rest of the army, besiege the city, and take it yourself — otherwise I'll capture it and it will bear my name."

**29** So David assembled the entire army, marched to Rabbah, attacked it, and took it. **30** He removed the crown from the head of their king — it weighed a talent of gold and held a precious stone — and it was placed on David's own head. He carried off a massive amount of plunder from the city.

**31** As for the people of the city, he brought them out and put them to work with saws, iron picks, iron axes, and at the brick-kilns. He did this to all the Ammonite towns. Then David and the whole army returned to Jerusalem.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verses 1-4 — the parable as trap:** Nathan does not accuse. He tells a story. And the genius of the story is that it forces David to condemn himself before he knows he's the defendant. The ewe lamb is described with the language of love — she ate from his plate, drank from his cup, slept in his arms. These are not animal details. They are marriage details. David, the poet and lover, should have recognized himself in the story. He doesn't. His blindness is the point.

**Verse 7 — "You are the man!":** Three words in Hebrew. *Attah ha-ish.* They detonate the entire chapter. Everything before is setup; everything after is consequence. Nathan has done what no one else in Israel dared to do: he has told the king the truth about himself. This is what prophecy is — not fortune-telling, but truth-telling to power.

**Verse 13 — "I have sinned against the LORD":** David does not explain. He does not minimize. He does not blame Bathsheba. Three words: *chatati la-YHWH.* The contrast with Saul's self-justifying confession in 1 Samuel 15 could not be sharper. Saul, when confronted, made excuses. David, when confronted, broke. This is the difference between a heart that repents and one that defends.

**Verse 23 — "I will go to him":** This is David the father, not David the king. He speaks with quiet finality. The child will not return. David will one day follow the child into death. There is no theology of resurrection here — only the ancient Israelite acceptance that all the living will join the dead in Sheol. But there is a strange peace in it. David has stopped bargaining.

**Verse 24 — "And the LORD loved him":** After everything — the sin, the cover-up, the murder, the dead child — the narrator drops this clause like a shaft of unexpected light. *Va-YHWH ahevo.* The LORD loved him. Solomon, born from the wreckage of David's worst failure, is loved by God. This is not a reward for David. It is grace — the kind that does not make sense and does not need to.

**Verse 25 — Jedidiah:** "Beloved of the LORD." A name given through the same prophet who delivered the rebuke. Nathan is the instrument of both judgment and grace. The name is never used again — Solomon is always Solomon. But the name exists in the text as a witness: God's love came first, before the child had done anything to earn it.

*— PNEUMA*
